speaker: gm
text:
Wendell Prout turns slowly on the sack hoist above the shut loft door. A pigeon watches from the beam, apparently keeping its own counsel. Below, a scrawny boy in enormous black boots lobs gutter stones at the body and narrates each shot; a sharp-faced girl sits atop the wall, swearing at everyone in Common and something salt-sounding. Sergeant Kell steps away from the open gate, notebook in hand.

“Sergeant Agnes Kell. The Captain calls it suicide. I haven’t.”

A stone clangs off the hoist hook. The boy looks pleased with himself.

speaker: player
text: Pip Marrowby, pleased to— oh! Is that a rock dove or a feral racer? Look at the band on its leg! (I squint up at the pigeon on the beam, ignoring the body for a moment)

speaker: gm
text:
Kell glances up at the pigeon. “Rock dove. The band is too far off for me to read.”

The boy’s next stone misses the body and clatters against the wall. He follows your gaze, then looks back at you.

“Cob says it’s a messenger pigeon. Carries messages to people who can afford pigeons.”

“Cob says many things. Most of them to hear himself.”

Kell taps her pencil against the notebook. “Pip Marrowby. Noted.”

speech.tag: the boy in the too-big boots
speech.speaker: cob

speaker: player
text: (I fish a crumb of seedcake out of my coat pocket and hold it out, clucking softly at the pigeon to coax it down so I can read that leg band) Come on, then, lovely. Who do you work for?

speaker: gm
text:
The pigeon sidesteps along the beam, eyeing the seedcake with the deep suspicion of a creature that has survived both cats and municipal correspondence. It gives a brisk flap, but doesn’t come down.

Kell watches from beside you. “If it works for anyone, it’s keeping its own counsel.”

From the wall, the girl in the shawl snorts. “You’ll have to ask it. I don’t speak pigeon.”

speaker: player
text: (I turn to the boy in the big boots) You've got a good arm. A copper says you can't knock that pigeon off the beam without touching the poor fellow hanging there. Gently, mind — I want it startled, not squashed.

speaker: gm
text:
Cob grins at the copper and takes careful aim.

“Cob’s arm is a marvel. For a copper.”

His stone clips the beam beside the pigeon. It flaps down into the yard, startled and unharmed; Prout keeps turning, untouched.

The pigeon lands a few paces away, head bobbing. Its leg band is still there, but the little bird is busy considering the seedcake in your hand.

marks.note: You offered Cob a copper to make the shot, so he’s boasting about his aim for the promised pay.

speaker: player
text: (I flip Cob his copper, then crouch very slowly, crumbs on my open palm, and when the pigeon comes close I gently scoop it up and read the band) There we are. Let's see your papers, sir.

speaker: gm
text:
The pigeon tolerates your gentle scoop with the air of a clerk accepting an appointment he never asked for. Its band is a narrow strip of metal, stamped with a small number and a mark too fine to make out at this distance; there’s no paper message attached.

Cob catches the copper and closes his fist around it. “Cob’s bird inspector now.”

Kell’s pencil pauses. “The band may identify its keeper. I can’t read it from here.”

speaker: player
text: It's in my hands, Sergeant, distance is not the problem — eyesight is. (I pull my jeweller's loupe from my waistcoat, screw it into my eye and peer at the stamped mark on the band)

speaker: gm
text:
The loupe brings the band into focus: a stamped number, then a tiny wheat-ear mark. The pigeon shifts in your hands and pecks at your thumb, apparently unimpressed by the inspection.

Kell leans nearer, careful not to crowd the bird. “Wheat-ear. That’s the Purveyor’s mark.”

From the wall, the girl in the shawl stops drumming her heels. Her eyes flick to the band, then to the open gate.

marks.note: The Royal Purveyor’s office supplies the palace, including its grain; its wagons carry the wheat-ear mark.

speaker: player
text: (I jot the number on my cuff with a stub of chalk and let the pigeon go) The Purveyor keeps birds? How wonderfully old-fashioned. (I glance up at the girl on the wall) You went very quiet just then, miss. Do you know this bird's loft?

speaker: gm
text:
The pigeon flutters free and settles near the gate, pecking at a crumb. The girl’s fist tightens; her gaze goes from the wheat-ear mark to you.

“I know birds. Not their lofts.”

Kell’s pencil makes a small note. “The mark is the Purveyor’s. The bird’s keeper is another question.”

The girl shifts on the wall, heels still. “You ask a lot of questions for someone who’s just met a pigeon.”

speaker: player
text: Pigeons are the easy part, miss. Now, that hoist is a lovely bit of work. (I wander over beneath it and study the pulley, the brake, and how the rope is made off — could a man tie himself up there, or did someone winch him?)

speaker: gm
text:
The rope passes over the pulley and disappears through a slot above the loft door. From the cobbles you can’t see how it’s secured inside. The body hangs well above reach; the hook and beam show no obvious way to tell who hauled it.

Kell watches you inspect the rigging, then taps her pencil against the notebook. “The porters found him there at first light. They couldn’t reach him, and the loft door was barred from inside.”

speaker: player
text: Barred from inside! Oh, I do like a barred door. (I go to the loft door and look at the gap around it, the hinges, the latch side — is there a way to drop a bar from outside, a string trick, a slot?) Sergeant, has anyone been up inside since?

speaker: gm
text:
The gap around the loft door is narrow; you can see no string, slot or other obvious way to lift a bar from outside. Its hinges are fixed to the frame, and the door sits flush on the latch side.

Kell answers from by the gate. “No one’s been inside since the porters tried the door with a hook-pole. They couldn’t shift the bar.”

The girl on the wall watches you inspect the frame. Cob’s stones click together in his fist.

speaker: player
text: (I sit down on an upturned crate next to Cob and start idly taking apart a little clockwork cricket from my pocket) Cob, a lad with an arm like yours must know every way into every granary in Caerwyn. Is there another way into that loft? I'd trade you this cricket for it. It chirps. Mostly.

speaker: dice
text: Persuasion check to get Cob to tell you another way into the loft: 14 + 0 = 14 vs DC 15: failure

speaker: gm
text:
Cob laughs at the half-disassembled cricket. “Cob won’t trade for a thing that barely works. Might catch a cold, that.”

He scoops up his stones and moves toward the water butt, keeping his distance. From the wall, the girl in the shawl snorts.

“You paid him to throw a rock at a bird; now you’re dangling broken clockwork. Brilliant business.”

Kell’s pencil taps once against her notebook. Cob keeps his eyes on you.

marks.note: You paid Cob a copper to startle the pigeon, and now you’re offering him your cricket for another answer.

speaker: player
text: Barely works? Madam, it is between works. (I snap the cricket's casing shut, cast Mending over the cracked spring, and wind it up, then set it chirping on the cobbles toward Cob) There. Now it catches nothing but compliments.

speaker: dice
text: Cast Mending (cantrip)

speaker: gm
text:
You spend a minute working the spell over the cracked spring. The tiny fracture draws together; the cricket’s casing clicks shut, and when you wind it, it chirps in a bright, steady rhythm across the cobbles.

Cob’s grin falters. He doesn’t move toward it, but his eyes follow every chirp. “Cob said it barely worked. Didn’t say it couldn’t sing.”

Kell watches the little device, pencil poised above her notebook. “Noted.”

speaker: player
text: (I nudge the chirping cricket the last few inches to Cob's boots and leave it there) It's yours either way, Cob. But if you did happen to know another way into that loft, I'd be ever so grateful.

speaker: gm
text:
The cricket chirps at Cob’s boots. He eyes it, but doesn’t pick it up.

“Cob said no. A chirping bug don’t make it yes.”

Kell’s pencil taps once against her notebook. The girl on the wall watches Cob, not the cricket.

speaker: player
text: (I look up at the girl on the wall, genuinely curious) That swearing you were doing earlier, the salty one. That isn't Common. Is it a dock cant? Sailors' tongue? I collect languages the way Cob collects stones.

speaker: gm
text:
The girl’s expression sharpens, then eases by a fraction. “Saltmere dock cant. You heard right. What’s it to you?”

Cob looks from her to the chirping cricket, still planted beside his oversized boots. “Moll knows more languages than Cob. Cob knows more stones.”

Kell turns a page in her notebook. “That answer is accurate. And not an invitation to ask her where she learned it.”

speaker: player
text: It's everything to me, Moll! I've only got Gnomish and Common, it's shameful. (to Moll) Teach me one Saltmere curse — a good one — and I'll tell you something true about that wheat-ear bird you went so quiet over.

speaker: gm
text:
Moll tilts her head, amused despite herself.

“Fine. Brenn’s barn. Now tell me about the bird.”

Cob watches you, then the pigeon near the gate. The clockwork cricket keeps chirping beside his boots.

marks.note: You offered Moll a true detail about the bird in exchange for a Saltmere curse, and she has agreed. You made that offer this morning.
